title: Gatka, the moving prayer
hookLine: the Sikh martial art, practiced with sticks and swords, often as a moving meditation
last: DHARAM YUDH — FAIR, EVEN IN CONFLICT.

cards: A Sikh procession on a festival day. The road is cleared in a wide circle. A drum starts.

Two young people step into the space with wooden sticks and small round shields, and they begin to circle each other, feet light, sticks flashing, the crowd shouting. It looks like a fight. Then you notice their faces.
And sometimes their lips are moving. Today: gatka, the moving prayer.

teach.h: SOTI AND PHARI — STICK AND SHIELD.
teach.b: Gatka is the Sikh martial art. In its best-known form today, it's practiced with a wooden stick, the soti, and a small shield, the phari. Some practitioners also train with swords, spears and other traditional weapons.
It grew out of older fighting arts the Sikhs of the Gurus' time trained in, when the Khalsa had to defend itself.

Today gatka appears at nagar kirtans, the processions that carry the Guru Granth Sahib through the streets, and especially at Hola Mohalla in Anandpur, the spring festival of martial skill that tradition traces to Guru Gobind Singh.
There are gatka competitions and teams too, with rules, points and safety gear. But teachers often say scoring isn't the heart of it.
Gatka rests on footwork, a pattern of steps called the paintra. You learn balance and rhythm before you ever swing a stick.

teach.h: THE BODY MOVES, THE MIND REMEMBERS.
teach.b: And the movement, they say, should be done in remembrance: Waheguru in the breath, the Name kept in mind while the body moves.
That's why people call it a moving prayer. It's the saint-soldier in one practice. The body trained, strong and quick.
The mind still and remembering. And the point isn't to hurt anyone. It's to be ready, and steady, at the same time.

how: Gatka is taught in gurdwaras and Sikh youth groups; teams perform it at nagar kirtan processions and at Hola Mohalla in Anandpur, and practitioners often keep Waheguru in mind as they move.

games.q: you've just started learning gatka. the teacher hands you a stick. what do they have you learn first?
o: how to hit as hard as you can.
games.why: gatka rests on the paintra, the footwork. steadiness comes before the stick.

practice: If you're able, stand, and shift your weight slowly from one foot to the other, arms loose, as if you were holding a light stick.
Keep the breath slow, and with each step give the mind one word to rest on: a word you pray with, if you pray, or simply now. After a minute, come to stillness and sit.
